source.title: Learning and communication pressures in neural networks: Lessons from emergent communication

confidence_rationale: This is the peer-reviewed, archival successor to the four-page non-archival workshop paper that triggered this pull -- same second author, same argument, two years later, with the three mismatches worked through and their resolutions named. That alone repairs the source-quality objection the earlier entry recorded (0.62), which is why confidence rises from 0.66 to 0.70 despite this still being a review with no new data. Direction stays mixed for the same reason as before: it endorses ARC-099's premise that absent structure implies an absent constraint, while naming constraints the inventory does not contain. What it adds is specificity about WHICH repairs worked -- population heterogeneity (Rita et al. 2022) and sender-receiver coupling (Michel et al. 2023) -- and one honest negative: no successful causal manipulation of MEMORY in neural agents is reported. Confidence is held at 0.70 rather than higher partly because of a discrepancy this pull could not resolve: the review glosses Michel et al. 2023 as tying sender and receiver into 'a single agent', whereas that paper's own abstract frames its mechanism as partitioning agents into pairs to limit CO-ADAPTATION. Those are different claims with different implications for role alternation, and the full paper could not be read (see mapping_caveat).
failure_signatures: Neural networks have no memory constraint to speak of -- the review states they 'have virtually no memory constraints because they are commonly heavily over-parametrized' -- and the one attempt it cites at imposing one by reducing parameters toward the theoretical minimum (Resnick et al. 2020) is not reported as successful, because over-parametrisation is itself load-bearing for trainability. A V6-entry item reading 'bounded memory' currently has no known implementation in this class of agent.

The review names the standard design as one where 'most emergent communication simulations keep senders and receivers distinct (i.e., agents that produce never comprehend, and vice versa)', against the human fact that anyone who can produce a language can also understand it. A V6 ecology assembled from off-the-shelf referential-game components inherits that split silently.

Three human/neural mismatches are enumerated -- ease-of-learning (replicates), generalisation (does not fully), group size (does not) -- and each was resolved only by adding a theoretically-motivated inductive bias after the fact. The pattern is that the missing ingredient was never visible in advance from the capability inventory, which is the structural problem with certifying a V6 ecology by checklist.

The review's causal claims are inherited from the primary literature, not measured here; 'not fully replicated' remains unquantified in this version too, and the reader has to go to Rita et al. 2022 for the numbers. Confidence in any inventory amendment should be taken from those primaries, not from this synthesis.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Reviewing three cases where the emergent linguistic behaviour of neural agents mismatched humans, the authors argue each was resolved by introducing a theoretically-motivated inductive bias, and identify the key pressures at play in language learning and emergence: communicative success, production effort, learnability, and psycho-/sociolinguistic factors. Among the resolutions named: population heterogeneity via differing agent learning rates recovers part of the group-size effect (Rita et al. 2022), and introducing sender-receiver ties recovers it further (Michel et al. 2023). Memory is identified as a human constraint neural agents lack, with no successful manipulation reported.
mapping.ree_translation: This is the archival version of the argument that prompted a re-examination of ARC-099's inventory, and reading it changes what weight the argument can bear. The claim that a V6 ecology's constraints -- not its architecture -- explain absent structure is endorsed by people running the human experiments, now in a peer-reviewed venue. The two additions proposed in the 2022 workshop paper survive into this version, but with different evidential status from each other, and ARC-099 should treat them differently. ROLE ALTERNATION, or more precisely a production/comprehension tie within one agent, now has an artificial-agent result behind it and the review reports it recovering the group-size effect. BOUNDED MEMORY does not: the review's own account is that neural agents lack memory constraints because they are over-parametrised, that reducing parameters toward a minimum is not a workable route, and no study is cited in which memory was successfully constrained and structure improved. So the honest disposition for governance is asymmetric -- the role-alternation gap has evidence and a named mechanism; the bounded-memory gap has a plausible story, a human-side theoretical rationale (see the Raviv 2019 Cognition entry, where compressibility pressure is located in limited memory capacity but shown to be deliverable by partner number instead), and no artificial-agent demonstration at all.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This remains a review with no new data, so every empirical claim is inherited and every effect size has to be read off the primaries. One specific discrepancy could not be resolved in this pull and is recorded rather than smoothed over: the review describes Michel et al. (2023) as introducing sender-receiver ties 'such that a sender and a receiver together form a single agent', which reads as role unification and would be direct support for a role-alternation condition. Michel et al.'s own published abstract instead describes 'partitioning the agents into sender-receiver pairs and limiting co-adaptation across pairs' -- a mechanism about restricting which pairs interact, which if anything REDUCES partner mixing and would be evidence for a different condition entirely. The full paper is hosted on OpenReview behind a browser-verification wall and was not read for this entry, so which reading is correct is left open. Anyone amending ARC-099's inventory on the strength of the role-alternation argument should read Michel et al. 2023 in full first; this is the same 'verify against the primary source' discipline that produced this pull. Finally, the target-mismatch caveat from the 2022 entry still applies: these authors care whether simulations are valid models of human language evolution, while ARC-099 cares whether a V6 signalling probe would be non-vacuous. [2026-09-24 follow-up chip, still UNRESOLVED] Full text remains inaccessible: exhausted arXiv (export.arxiv.org API, both title and author search, 0 results -- confirmed no arXiv version exists), Mathieu Rita's own publications page (abstract only, no PDF/code link), Semantic Scholar's API record for this exact paper (openAccessPdf.url is empty, no license), OpenReview direct-PDF and API routes (both return the bot-verification ChallengeRequiredError, not bypassed per instruction), the ICLR 2023 virtual-site poster page (links only back to the blocked OpenReview forum), and a Papers-with-Code search (no match). One partial, honest data point: the paper's OWN public abstract (independently confirmed via the ICLR/mlanthology.org listing and a fresh WebSearch, not merely the review's gloss) states the mechanism as 'partitioning the agents into sender-receiver pairs and limiting co-adaptation across pairs' -- i.e. it is Michel et al.'s own words, not only the review's paraphrase, that describe reading (b) rather than a 'single agent' merge. This weighs against reading (a) but does NOT settle the discrepancy: the abstract does not state whether any agent ever occupies both sender and receiver roles (the operational role-alternation test) or whether the pairing is implemented via tied parameters/gradient blocking versus merely restricted interaction topology -- that requires the method section, which remains unread. Treat the discrepancy as still open.
mapping.source_context: Peer-reviewed review article synthesising deep-learning emergent-communication simulations (Lewis and referential games), large language models, and human language-evolution experiments. No new data.

confidence_components.notes: Source quality 0.70, up from the 0.62 recorded for the same argument in its 2022 workshop form: this version is peer reviewed, archival, and long enough to name the specific studies and resolutions rather than gesturing at a literature. It is still a review with no new data, which caps it well below the primary entries in this directory. Mapping fidelity 0.82, the highest here, because the paper's organising question -- which inductive biases must be supplied for an artificial multi-agent system to produce human-like emergent structure -- is ARC-099's question almost verbatim. Transfer risk 0.40 reflects the unresolved Michel et al. discrepancy noted in the caveat: a review's gloss on a primary result is exactly the kind of link this pull exists to check, and one link in this chain is still unchecked. [2026-09-24] A dedicated follow-up chip tried to obtain the full text and could not (all routes exhausted -- see mapping_caveat); confidence numbers are left unchanged because the underlying uncertainty is unchanged, not reduced -- the one new data point (the paper's own abstract, not just the review's gloss) nudges toward reading (b) but does not close the gap the transfer_risk score is pricing in.
